description: Caterpillar Inc. provides construction and mining equipment, off-highway diesel and natural gas engines, industrial gas turbines, and diesel-electric locomotives in the United States and international
description_full: Caterpillar Inc. provides construction and mining equipment, off-highway diesel and natural gas engines, industrial gas turbines, and diesel-electric locomotives in the United States and internationally. The Construction Industries segment offers asphalt pavers, cold planers, compactors, forestry machines, material handlers, motor graders, pipelayers, road reclaimers, telehandlers, track-type tractors, and track and wheel excavators; backhoe, compact track, skid steer, track-type, and wheel loaders; and related parts and work tools. Its Resource Industries segment provides electric rope and hydraulic shovels, draglines, rotary drills, hard rock vehicles, mining trucks, wheel loaders, off-highway and articulated trucks, wide-body trucks, wheel tractor scrapers and dozers, and landfill and soil compactors; machinery components, and wear and maintenance components; and technology products and services for fleet management, equipment management analytics, autonomous machine capabilities, safety services, and mining performance solutions. The Energy & Transportation segment offers reciprocating engine powered generator sets; reciprocating engines, drivetrain, and integrated systems and solutions; centrifugal gas compressors and related services; and diesel-electric locomotive components, and other rail-related products. Its Financial Products segment provides operating and finance leases, revolving charge accounts, installment sale contracts, repair/rebuild financing, working capital loans, and wholesale financing; and insurance and risk management products and services. The All Other segment offers parts distribution; logistics and distribution services; electronics and control systems; dealer portfolio management; brand management and marketing strategy; and digital investment services. It also provides mining software solutions. The company was formerly known as Caterpillar Tractor Co. Caterpillar Inc. was incorporated in 1925 and is headquartered in Irving, Texas.
ceo_bio: Mr. Joseph E. Creed CPA | Chairman & CEO | Age 49 | Compensation: $4.4M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 118K people. Revenue per employee of $573K ranks in the top quartile among Industrials peers. Each employee generates $76K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $2K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 8× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: Caterpillar, Inc. is a mega-cap industrials business with a $255.6B market cap on $67.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 18% against a 9% cost of capital — a 9-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $8.9B in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.32× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 2.0× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 6.1×.

Shareholder yield of 3.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 16% operating margin runs 8pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.50x).
It accounts for 1.7% of sector revenue and 2.6% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+6.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 52% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 35% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 48% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 41% and a beta of 1.04, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $1.9B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 39% in the 2020 crash, 30% in the 2022 bear market and 73% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $467 (margin of safety -20%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 24%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $342 to $642 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: EV/EBITDA 16.7 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 28.7 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 77% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 26 covering analysts target $823 on average, 47% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 18% clears the cost of capital of 9.2% by 9pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.46).
It converts 13% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.32x.
ROE of 42% is amplified by 4.6x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 3.2% of revenue on R&D and 0.4% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.0x net debt to EBITDA ($10.0B of cash against $36.2B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.1x.
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 1.9 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.4% over 3 years, 10.1% over 5 years and 3.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 18%).
At current returns, reinvesting 36% of profits supports about 6.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 10.8% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.22 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 45% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 43%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.2x, 4.2% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 23, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 74%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 14 sales over the past year, net $25.6M sold.
It returns 3.1% a year to shareholders (2.0% in buybacks and 1.2% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.1% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 44 consecutive years, raising it 4.2% a year over the last five.
people: With about 118,000 employees, each generates about $573K of revenue, 1.6x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 4.7% a year.
That works out to $76K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.4M (8x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
